DiffusionOPD in Gollek

Install Blog GitHub

DiffusionOPD in Gollek

Gollek now has a dedicated Java-first scaffold for DiffusionOPD, a multi-task on-policy distillation method for diffusion models.

Citation:

  • Quanhao Li, Junqiu Yu, Kaixun Jiang, Yujie Wei, Zhen Xing, Pandeng Li, Ruihang Chu, Shiwei Zhang, Yu Liu, Zuxuan Wu. DiffusionOPD: A Unified Perspective of On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models. arXiv:2605.15055, 2026. arXiv

Why this matters

Gollek is a one-stop Java platform for inference, ML, DL, and NN training. That means diffusion alignment work should follow the same rule:

  • training APIs in Java
  • orchestration in Java
  • datasets and task routing in Java
  • backend bridges only where runners or kernels already need them

DiffusionOPD fits that direction well because the paper’s core idea is an algorithmic training loop, not a Python-only runtime requirement.

What was added

New Java modules

  • :ml:gollek-ml-diffusion-api
  • :ml:gollek-ml-diffusion-opd

Main Java entrypoints

  • tech.kayys.gollek.train.diffusion.api.*
  • tech.kayys.gollek.train.diffusion.opd.DefaultDiffusionOpdTrainer
  • tech.kayys.gollek.train.diffusion.opd.adapter.RunnerDiffusionAdapters
  • tech.kayys.gollek.ml.Gollek.DL.diffusionOpdTrainer()

Module roles

gollek-ml-diffusion-api

This module provides the stable contracts:

  • DiffusionTask
  • DiffusionPromptSample
  • DiffusionDenoiser
  • DiffusionScheduler
  • DiffusionConditioningResolver
  • DiffusionOptimizationStep
  • DiffusionOpdConfig
  • DiffusionOpdSession

gollek-ml-diffusion-opd

This module provides the first algorithm scaffold:

  • DefaultDiffusionOpdTrainer
  • round-robin multi-task sampling
  • stage-aware teacher routing by timestep interval
  • scheduler-based transition mean adaptation
  • ODE/SDE loss shape for per-step mean matching
  • Java listener lifecycle hooks
  • checkpoint-directory summary/history artifacts
  • adapters from existing Gollek diffusion runner contracts

Current design

The current vertical slice focuses on the part Gollek needs first:

  1. represent diffusion OPD tasks in Java
  2. run student-teacher rollout supervision in Java
  3. map backend denoisers and schedulers into the OPD abstraction
  4. expose the builder through the canonical Gollek ML entrypoint

This is intentionally narrower than the full paper implementation. It gives Gollek a clean Java surface before more backend-specific logic is layered in.

First adapter layer

Gollek already has diffusion runner contracts under runner/gollek-diffusion, including:

  • UNetModel
  • Scheduler

Those can now be adapted into OPD training with:

DiffusionDenoiser student =
    RunnerDiffusionAdapters.denoiser(unetModel);

DiffusionScheduler diffusionScheduler =
    RunnerDiffusionAdapters.scheduler(ddimScheduler);

That keeps the algorithm Java-native while reusing existing Gollek runtime surfaces.

Example shape

var trainer = Gollek.DL.diffusionOpdTrainer()
    .samplerType(DiffusionSamplerType.ODE)
    .student(RunnerDiffusionAdapters.denoiser(studentUnet))
    .teacher("ocr", RunnerDiffusionAdapters.denoiser(ocrTeacherUnet))
    .teacher("aesthetic", RunnerDiffusionAdapters.denoiser(aestheticTeacherUnet))
    .scheduler(RunnerDiffusionAdapters.scheduler(ddimScheduler))
    .conditioningResolver(sample -> textEncoder.encode(sample.prompt()))
    .task(new DiffusionTask("ocr", "OCR", "ocr", "teacher-ocr", ocrPrompts))
    .task(new DiffusionTask("aesthetic", "Aesthetic", "aesthetic", "teacher-aesthetic", aestheticPrompts))
    .maxRounds(100)
    .batchSize(2)
    .build();

trainer.fit();

The exact text-encoder, optimizer step, checkpointing, and variance handling will keep evolving, but the Java module boundaries are now in place.

There is also a concrete Java example in the repo:

  • gollek/training/gollek-train-examples/src/main/java/tech/kayys/gollek/train/examples/DiffusionOpdDDIMExample.java

And a JBang script for fast local experimentation:

  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_diffusion_opd_ddim.java

When checkpointDir(...) is set, the current scaffold now writes:

  • diffusion-opd-summary.json
  • diffusion-opd-history.csv
  • diffusion-opd-report.json

It also supports Java-side lifecycle callbacks through DiffusionOpdListener.

For stage-aware routing, each DiffusionTask can now carry DiffusionTeacherBinding entries such as:

new DiffusionTask(
    "ocr",
    "OCR",
    "ocr",
    "teacher-ocr",
    List.of(
        new DiffusionTeacherBinding("ocr-early", 0, 2, "early"),
        new DiffusionTeacherBinding("ocr-late", 2, Integer.MAX_VALUE, "late")
    ),
    promptSamples
)

This is the current Gollek implementation step most directly inspired by eDiff-I’s stage-specialized denoiser idea.

The trainer now also supports per-stage loss weighting, so early, mid, and late teachers can contribute with different emphasis during OPD. For common setups, Gollek provides Java helpers through DiffusionTeacherBindings, for example:

new DiffusionTask(
    "ocr",
    "OCR",
    "ocr",
    "teacher-ocr",
    DiffusionTeacherBindings.splitEarlyLate(
        4,
        "ocr-early",
        "ocr-late",
        1.25d,
        0.85d
    ),
    promptSamples
)

This keeps stage routing configuration in Java while making the training loop more flexible than fixed hardcoded intervals.

Gollek also now supports scheduler-aware partitioning. Instead of splitting stages by raw step count, bindings can be derived from the scheduler timetable itself, which is a better fit for sparse samplers such as DDIM:

var diffusionScheduler = RunnerDiffusionAdapters.scheduler(ddimScheduler);

var bindings = DiffusionTeacherBindings.splitEarlyLate(
    diffusionScheduler,
    "ocr-early",
    "ocr-late",
    1.25d,
    0.85d
);

This keeps the API Java-native while letting stage boundaries follow the effective denoising schedule rather than assuming uniform step spacing.

Gollek also now supports adaptive stage weighting in the trainer. When enabled, the OPD loop tracks per-stage mean loss and rebalances stage factors across rounds, which helps emphasize underperforming denoising regions without throwing away the base stage weights configured in DiffusionTeacherBinding.

var trainer = Gollek.DL.diffusionOpdTrainer()
    .adaptiveStageWeighting(true)
    .adaptiveStageWeightMomentum(0.60d)
    .adaptiveStageWeightRange(0.80d, 1.35d)
    .build();

Current behavior:

  • stage factors start at 1.0
  • each round computes per-stage mean base loss
  • higher-loss stages are nudged upward within the configured factor range
  • lower-loss stages are nudged downward, with momentum smoothing

Gollek also now has a dedicated alignment seam for the safetensor-native Stable Diffusion inference runner in StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters. The current status is:

  • PNDMScheduler is directly bridged for timestep/schedule alignment
  • stable-diffusion-native UNet adaptation is available through an explicit TensorAccelBridge
  • this keeps training and inference aligned without pretending the core Tensor and AccelTensor stacks are already the same runtime

Example shape:

var scheduler = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.scheduler(pndmScheduler);

var denoiser = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.denoiser(
    stableDiffusionUnet,
    tensorAccelBridge
);

For float32 experimentation, Gollek also provides a bridge helper so callers only need to supply two explicit conversions:

var bridge = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.float32Bridge(
    coreTensor -> extractFloat32(coreTensor),
    (values, shape) -> createCoreTensor(values, shape)
);

This keeps the adapter usable today while Gollek’s generic core-tensor materialization API is still maturing.

For the Metal-aligned stable-diffusion-native path, Gollek now also provides a no-friction convenience overload:

MetalBinding.initialize();
MetalBinding metalBinding = MetalBinding.getInstance();
metalBinding.init();

var bridge = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.metalDefaultTensorFloat32Bridge(
    metalBinding
);

This overload returns an accelerator-aware bridge that:

  • materializes stable-diffusion-native AccelTensor values into core DefaultTensor objects tagged as DeviceType.METAL
  • exposes Metal runtime metadata such as device name, unified-memory status, native availability, and available accelerator memory
  • keeps the Java training stack aligned with the maintained gollek-backend-metal binding surface without depending on stale backend adapter classes

Current caveat:

  • the materialized core tensor is a transport tensor for adapter boundaries and should receive a full execution backend before downstream math operations are invoked

Gollek now also supports an executable scheduler bridge for the stable-diffusion-native PNDM path:

var bridge = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.metalDefaultTensorFloat32Bridge(
    metalBinding
);

DiffusionScheduler scheduler = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.scheduler(
    pndmScheduler,
    bridge
);

This means OPD training code can now reuse the same Java-side scheduler step shape that the stable-diffusion-native inference runner uses, instead of only reading scheduler metadata.

Gollek also now includes an end-to-end structural trainer demo that uses both stable-diffusion-native bridge surfaces together:

var trainer = Gollek.DL.diffusionOpdTrainer()
    .student(StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.denoiser(studentUnet, bridge))
    .teacher("ocr-early", StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.denoiser(ocrEarlyTeacher, bridge))
    .scheduler(StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.scheduler(pndmScheduler, bridge))
    .task(...)
    .build();

This is still a Java-first scaffold rather than full weight-backed Stable Diffusion training, but it proves that:

  • the UNet adapter and scheduler adapter compose cleanly inside the OPD trainer
  • stage-aware routing and adaptive weighting still work on the stable-diffusion-native path
  • Gollek can keep training and inference aligned without leaving Java at the orchestration level

To prepare the jump from stub fixtures to real local weights, the example lane now validates the native runner repository layout and reports whether a local fixture is usable. The expected structure matches the current StableDiffusionNativeRunner:

  • text_encoder/
  • unet/
  • vae/
  • tokenizer/

The examples auto-detect common local paths and also accept an override via GOLLEK_SD_NATIVE_MODEL_DIR or a direct path argument.

Gollek now also includes a plain-Java fixture loader utility for this lane, so the stable-diffusion-native trainer example can automatically switch from a stub UNet to a real local unet/ safetensor checkpoint when the fixture is available.

That lane now also supports per-role fixture resolution, so student, ocr-early, ocr-late, aesthetics-early, and aesthetics-late can point to different local repos through dedicated environment overrides or role-named subdirectories under a shared base fixture.

When the shared fixture is usable, the example can also upgrade prompt conditioning from a synthetic tensor to real CLIP text embeddings loaded from text_encoder/ plus tokenizer/, while still keeping role-specific UNet fixtures separate.

That real CLIP conditioning path now exists in both the Gradle example and the JBang example, so quick local experimentation follows the same native bridge behavior as the main Java example lane.

Gollek now also supports task-specific text-conditioning fixtures in that example lane. ocr and aesthetics can each resolve their own CLIP/text encoder repo through environment overrides such as GOLLEK_SD_NATIVE_MODEL_DIR_TEXT_OCR and GOLLEK_SD_NATIVE_MODEL_DIR_TEXT_AESTHETICS, or through text-ocr/ and text-aesthetics/ subdirectories under a shared fixture root.

Those task-specific conditioning lanes are now also written into the standard DiffusionOPD artifacts. The summary JSON and round-history CSV can include fields such as conditioningTaskModes, conditioningTaskFixtureBaseDirs, and conditioningTaskFixtures, so loss analysis can stay tied to the actual text-conditioning source used per task.

The native bridge examples now also record observed runtime diagnostics instead of only configured fixture metadata. Artifact fields such as conditioningTaskResolveCounts, conditioningTaskLossSteps, conditioningTaskLossSums, and conditioningTaskMeanLoss show how often each conditioning lane actually ran and how its per-task loss profile evolved.

That runtime path is now formalized through DiffusionOpdRuntimeObserver, so integrations can attach training-time diagnostics to the standard DiffusionOPD summary/history artifacts without relying on example-owned mutable metadata maps.

Gollek now also ships a reusable built-in implementation, ConditioningTaskMetricsObserver, inside gollek-ml-diffusion-opd. That observer captures per-task conditioning lane usage and loss aggregates so integrations can adopt standard conditioning diagnostics without rewriting their own observer class.

Alongside it, Gollek now includes TeacherStageTaskMetricsObserver, a second built-in runtime observer for standard OPD rollout aggregation. It captures observed task, teacher, stage, and task-stage usage/loss metrics so diffusion integrations can attach a fuller diagnostics bundle with just a couple of observer registrations.

To reduce that wiring further, Gollek now provides DiffusionOpdDiagnosticsPacks.standardTaskDiagnostics(...) plus DefaultDiffusionOpdTrainer.Builder.runtimeObservers(...), so integrations can enable the standard conditioning and rollout diagnostics bundle in a single builder call.

The trainer now also emits a normalized diffusion-opd-report.json artifact next to the summary and history files. That report groups run metadata, artifacts, teacher/stage/task diagnostics, conditioning diagnostics, adaptive weighting details, and round history into clearer top-level sections for downstream analysis.

That normalized report schema is now represented by small typed records in the DiffusionOPD API, including DiffusionOpdReport, DiffusionOpdRunReport, and DiffusionOpdArtifactsReport, so downstream Java tooling can align to stable top-level sections instead of depending on ad hoc string-key conventions alone.

Gollek now also exposes DiffusionOpdReports.load(...) in gollek-ml-diffusion-opd, so Java integrations can read diffusion-opd-report.json back into the typed report schema instead of only writing it.

For terminal-first workflows, the repo now also includes a JBang inspector:

  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_diffusion_opd_report_inspector.java

It loads diffusion-opd-report.json through DiffusionOpdReports.load(...) and can print either the full report or selected sections such as overview, run, teachers, conditioning, or roundHistory directly from the terminal, in either plain text or pretty-printed JSON.

The inspector now also supports focused history selectors such as roundHistory:last, roundHistory:task=ocr, roundHistory:teacher=ocr-early, roundHistory:stage=early, and roundHistory:round=2, which makes it easier to inspect one slice of OPD behavior without dumping the entire history array.

That selector path now supports compact chained queries too, for example roundHistory:task=ocr:last, roundHistory:teacher=ocr-early:last, roundHistory:task=ocr:count, and roundHistory:task=ocr:meanLoss, so terminal inspection can return one row or one aggregate instead of a full list.

It also supports ranked slices such as roundHistory:task=ocr:sort=-averageLoss:top=3 or roundHistory:teacher=ocr-early:sort=round:top=5, which is handy when you want the worst-loss rows or the earliest/latest few entries from a filtered subset.

For a more compact terminal view, the inspector now also supports summary presets such as taskSummary=ocr, teacherSummary=ocr-early, and stageSummary=early. Those return a small aggregate bundle with count, mean loss, the latest matching row, and a few representative ranked entries.

The summary layer also supports paired comparisons such as taskTeacherSummary=ocr,ocr-early, taskStageSummary=ocr,early, and teacherStageSummary=ocr-early,early, which makes it easier to inspect one combined slice without manually chaining multiple filters.

For bulk comparison, the inspector now also supports grouped rollups such as taskSummaries, teacherSummaries, and stageSummaries, each returning one aggregate map keyed by the discovered task, teacher, or stage values in the report history.

Those grouped rollups can now be ranked too, for example with taskSummaries:sort=-meanLoss:top=5 or teacherSummaries:sort=-count:top=3, which makes it easier to surface the most problematic or most-active slices directly from the terminal.

The same idea now works for combined dimensions too with taskTeacherSummaries, taskStageSummaries, and teacherStageSummaries, including ranked forms such as taskTeacherSummaries:sort=-meanLoss:top=10.

The inspector now also supports table and csv output modes for these summary views, which makes it easier to move from terminal inspection into spreadsheet or dashboard workflows without writing a separate export script.

Those export-oriented modes now also support optional column projection, so a command can request a compact schema such as value,count,meanLoss or pair,count,meanLoss instead of exporting every available field.

The inspector can now also write text, json, table, or csv output directly to a file path from the CLI. It can infer export format from output filenames such as .json, .csv, .table, .md, .txt, or .log, and _ remains available as a no-projection placeholder when a call shape still needs it.

Projection now also understands a few friendly aliases and flattened latest-row fields, including loss, latestRound, latestLoss, latestTeacher, latestTask, latestStage, top1Round, top1Loss, first1Round, and first1Loss.

For common export views, the inspector now also supports small projection presets such as minimal, compact, latest, leaderboard, details, and compare, which expand to reusable column sets for table and csv output.

The richer details preset and pair-oriented compare preset now also flatten one representative top-loss row and one representative first-round row through aliases such as top1Round, top1Loss, first1Round, and first1Loss.

Those presets are now section-aware too: grouped single-dimension summaries expand around value, while pair rollups such as taskTeacherSummaries expand around pair.

For repeated analysis workflows, the inspector now also supports directory-oriented bundle export through selectors like bundle=standard and bundle=rollups, so one command can emit a small pack of related JSON, CSV, table, or text views into an output directory. Each bundle now also includes a manifest.json index describing the bundle type, creation timestamp, format, source report path, and per-file section metadata for generated files. For table and csv bundles, grouped summaries default to compact projection and pair rollups default to compare projection unless an explicit column selection is supplied. Ad hoc packs are supported too through bundle=custom:overview,taskSummaries,taskTeacherSummaries, and custom entries can assign output aliases through section@alias, such as bundle=custom:overview@run-overview,taskTeacherSummaries@teacher-pairs. Custom entries can also override their own projection through #columns, for example bundle=custom:taskSummaries@tasks#compact,taskTeacherSummaries@pairs#compare. They can also override per-entry format through !json, !csv, !table, or !text, for example bundle=custom:overview@run-overview!json,taskTeacherSummaries@teacher-pairs#compare!csv. Bundle directories and manifest.json files can also be inspected directly through the same inspector entrypoint, including manifest, bundleSummary, bundleHealth, files, and file:<name> views, plus filtered file lists such as files:format=csv and files:section=taskTeacherSummaries. Bundle manifests can also be summarized through grouped selectors like filesSummary:by=section, filesSummary:by=format:sort=-count, or filesSummary:by=section:sort=-count:top=3. bundleSummary adds a compact overview with total file count, section count, format count, and the dominant section/format rows, and also supports focus=sections|formats|all plus top=<n> for smaller embedded rollups. dominant=true trims the output down to the headline section/format winners without the embedded summary lists. It also validates the manifest against the bundle directory and reports existingFileCount, missingFileCount, and missingFiles when bundle artifacts are missing on disk. bundleHealth provides the same integrity signal in a smaller status-oriented shape with healthy, normalized status, healthScore, alertLevel, stable issueCodes, primaryIssueCode, compact healthBadge with UI-ready variant, label, token, tooltip, checkStatus, primaryCheckCode, and primaryCheckSeverity, human-facing summaryMessage and recommendedAction, missingFileCount, missingFiles, plus grouped missingSections and missingFormats. It also exposes structured checks for named validations like output-directory presence and artifact completeness, normalized checkSummary fields (total, passed, failed, passRate, failureRate, status, alertLevel, local summaryMessage, local recommendedAction, local issueCodes, local primaryIssueCode, nested healthBadge with status, alertLevel, primaryIssueCode, primaryCheckName, primaryCheckMessage, primaryCheckSeverity, score, variant, label, token, checkStatus, summaryMessage, recommendedAction, and tooltip, dominantSeverity, allPassed, hasCriticalFailures, hasWarningFailures, hasInfoFailures, failingSeverityCounts, primaryFailingName, primaryFailingCode, primaryFailingSeverity, primaryFailingMessage, failingNames, failingCodes, and severityCounts), along with failingChecks, failingCheckCount, and aggregate counters such as passingCheckCount, criticalCheckCount, warningCheckCount, and infoCheckCount for compact status summaries. The health view also supports focus=files|sections|formats|all and top=<n> for more compact diagnosis slices. The inspector can also load the actual generated artifact chosen by exact name or by a filter, for example loadfile:overview.json or loadfile:format=csv:section=taskTeacherSummaries. When a filter matches multiple files, sort=name|-name|section|format|count, top=<n>, pick=first|last, or index=<n> can be added for stable selection.

Concrete examples are now included in the repo:

  • gollek/training/gollek-train-examples/src/main/java/tech/kayys/gollek/train/examples/DiffusionOpdStableDiffusionMetalBridgeExample.java
  • gollek/training/gollek-train-examples/src/main/java/tech/kayys/gollek/train/examples/DiffusionOpdStableDiffusionNativeBridgeTrainerExample.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_diffusion_opd_stable_diffusion_metal_bridge.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_diffusion_opd_stable_diffusion_native_bridge.java

For Apple accelerator alignment, Gollek now also supports a Metal-aware bridge factory backed by gollek-backend-metal metadata:

var metalBridge = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.metalFloat32Bridge(
    MetalBinding.getInstance(),
    coreTensor -> extractFloat32(coreTensor),
    (values, shape) -> createCoreTensor(values, shape)
);

This does not pretend Tensor and AccelTensor are zero-copy identical yet, but it does let OPD integrations carry real Metal backend capability signals such as device name, unified-memory status, and available accelerator memory.

Gollek now also has a DefaultTensor materializer path for backend-aware bridges. This means callers can provide a concrete ComputeBackend plus target DeviceType, and the adapter will build core tensors with that backend attached instead of only handing back raw float32 construction callbacks:

var bridge = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.defaultTensorFloat32Bridge(
    computeBackend,
    DeviceType.METAL,
    coreTensor -> extractFloat32(coreTensor)
);

There is also a Metal-specific convenience variant:

var bridge = StableDiffusionRunnerAdapters.metalDefaultTensorFloat32Bridge(
    MetalBinding.getInstance(),
    computeBackend,
    coreTensor -> extractFloat32(coreTensor)
);

Related papers and how they help Gollek

Not every diffusion paper helps the same layer of the stack. For Gollek, these papers split into four practical buckets:

1. Core distillation objective

  • DiffusionOPD: Quanhao Li et al., DiffusionOPD: A Unified Perspective of On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models, arXiv:2605.15055, 2026.

This is the main paper behind the current Java scaffold. It tells us how to:

  • structure teacher-student multi-task diffusion training
  • supervise on the student’s own rollout
  • use per-step mean matching instead of higher-variance PPO-style gradients
  • unify deterministic ODE and stochastic SDE supervision

For Gollek, this paper should continue driving:

  • DefaultDiffusionOpdTrainer
  • TransitionMeanAdapter
  • DiffusionOpdLosses
  • teacher registry and multi-task sampling

2. Latent diffusion architecture foundation

  • LDM: Robin Rombach et al., High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models, arXiv:2112.10752, 2022.

This is the architectural baseline that matters most for Gollek’s diffusion runtime. It tells us why latent-space training and cross-attention conditioning are the right default path for a practical Java platform.

For Gollek, this paper should drive:

  • stronger latent diffusion abstractions in runner/gollek-diffusion
  • explicit text-conditioning interfaces
  • separation of autoencoder, denoiser, and scheduler contracts
  • future checkpoint/model manifest structure for latent diffusion pipelines

3. Multi-stage denoiser specialization

  • eDiff-I: Yogesh Balaji et al., eDiff-I: Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with an Ensemble of Expert Denoisers, arXiv:2211.01324, 2023.

This paper is especially interesting for Gollek because it says different denoising stages behave differently, and that stage-specialized denoisers can improve text alignment without raising total inference cost.

For Gollek, this suggests a strong next improvement after basic OPD:

  • extend DiffusionTask or the future teacher registry with timestep-range specialization
  • support stage-aware teacher routing
  • allow different teachers or adapters for early, mid, and late denoising
  • expose this as a Java composition strategy instead of a monolithic single teacher

This is probably the most useful paper here after DiffusionOPD itself.

4. Production-grade latent diffusion conditioning

  • SDXL: Dustin Podell et al., SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis, arXiv:2307.01952, 2023.

SDXL is less about the OPD loss itself and more about what a stronger practical latent diffusion backbone looks like:

  • larger UNet
  • richer conditioning
  • multiple text encoders
  • multi-aspect-ratio training
  • refinement model

For Gollek, this suggests future improvements to the Java diffusion runtime:

  • richer conditioning resolver contracts
  • support for multiple conditioning streams
  • optional refiner-stage modeling
  • better pipeline metadata for base-plus-refiner flows

5. Editing and image-to-image behavior

  • SDEdit: Chenlin Meng et al., SDEdit: Guided Image Synthesis and Editing with Stochastic Differential Equations, arXiv:2108.01073, 2022.

This one is useful, but for a narrower slice. It matters most if Gollek wants:

  • image-to-image editing
  • partial-noise inversion/editing workflows
  • faithfulness-vs-realism controls

For the current DiffusionOPD training work, it is secondary. It becomes important once Gollek exposes editing-style diffusion pipelines in Java.

Priority order for Gollek

If we prioritize by what improves the current Java diffusion roadmap the most:

  1. 2605.15055 / DiffusionOPD
    • continue implementing the real training loop
  2. 2211.01324 / eDiff-I
    • add stage-aware teacher specialization
  3. 2112.10752 / LDM
    • harden the latent diffusion runtime architecture
  4. 2307.01952 / SDXL
    • extend conditioning, aspect ratio, and refiner support
  5. 2108.01073 / SDEdit
    • add editing workflows later

Best next code improvement from these papers

The highest-value next code step inspired by this paper set is:

  • add stage-aware teacher routing to DiffusionOPD

Why:

  • it directly combines the current OPD scaffold with eDiff-I’s strongest idea
  • it fits Gollek’s Java-first modular design well
  • it can be expressed cleanly as timestep-range routing without forcing a new training abstraction

That means future Gollek changes should likely introduce:

  • timestep-interval teacher bindings
  • a teacher selector that picks the teacher by task plus denoising stage
  • stage-specific metadata in summary/history artifacts

This is the most natural research-driven improvement after the current listener/checkpoint/example work.
